title: The Hidden Advantage of Mask Resampling:A Theory of Masked Autoencoders

paper.title: The Hidden Advantage of Mask Resampling: A Theory of Masked Autoencoders
paper.abstract: Abstract Why can masked prediction learn useful representations that unmasked reconstruction misses? We study this question in a high-dimensional model of a masked autoencoder (MAE) trained on data with shared latent structure and heterogeneous noise. We prove that masked linear reconstruction can recover the latent feature at linear sample complexity in regimes where unmasked linear reconstruction, equivalent to PCA, fails. The analysis also quantifies the statistical advantage of mask resampling, an established ingredient of masked pretraining. By introducing a fixed collection of K K masks per sample, we characterize its effect on feature recovery and downstream performance, identifying regimes where greater mask diversity lowers sample complexity. Guided by this prediction, we find that random cropping and flipping in standard image-training pipelines can obscure the advantage of mask resampling by renewing the prediction task even when the patch mask is fixed. Removing these transformations reveals a downstream advantage for dynamic over static masking in CNN autoencoders and vision transformers. A complementary BERT pilot finds benefits from greater mask diversity on downstream language tasks. Our results separate the benefit of the masked prediction objective from that of mask diversity, and show how a tractable theory can guide experiments that uncover advantages hidden by standard training practices.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Why can predicting missing parts of an input produce more useful representations than reconstructing the entire input? Building on denoising autoencoders [ 52 ] , Pathak et al. [46] predicted missing image regions from visible context and obtained more transferable representations than a standard autoencoder trained without input masking, a paradigm that now underlies masked language and image modeling [ 23 , 27 , 10 , 56 ] . Masked learning therefore couples two ingredients: a prediction objective that specifies what structure is rewarded, and an augmentation procedure that controls how many distinct prediction tasks a given sample ever presents. Despite its empirical success, our theoretical understanding of how these ingredients shape learned representations remains incomplete. We develop a high-dimensional theory that separates their effects and connects them to latent-feature recovery and downstream performance. Motivated by the observation that unmasked, i.e., the standard autoencoder, reconstruction 2 2 2 By unmasked reconstruction, we mean the standard autoencoder objective that observes the entire input and minimizes squared reconstruction error over all coordinates. can favor high-variance nuisance directions over downstream-relevant structure [ 9 ] , we consider a data model with a shared latent direction and heterogeneous coordinate-wise noise. The latent direction carries the downstream signal, while heterogeneity allows nuisance variance to dominate the leading principal component. Masking changes this competition by requiring hidden coordinates to be predicted from the visible ones, rather than rewarded for their own variance. We prove that a linear masked autoencoder recovers the latent direction with n = O ⁡ ( d ) n=O(d) samples where unmasked linear reconstruction , equivalent to PCA, fails ( Sec. 3 ). Figure 1: Isolating mask resampling reveals its contribution to representation learning. Downstream accuracy versus masking ratio ρ \rho for dynamic masking (blue), static masking (yellow), and unmasked reconstruction (red). (a) Shallow autoencoder on spiked model ( Sec. 2 ); curves are theory and markers are simulations. (b) CNN autoencoder on CIFAR-10 (test top-1). (c) ViT-Base on ImageNet-100 (validation top-5). In (b,c), blue and yellow curves use no stochastic cropping or flipping. The purple reference includes cropping and flipping with dynamic mask resampling at ρ = 0.625 \rho=0.625 (b) and ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 (c) . At suitable masking ratios, resampling alone reaches comparable accuracy. Bars and shading show ± 1 \pm 1 standard deviation (SD). See App. H for details. Analyzing this model clearly reveals a second notable effect: the number of distinct masks available per sample controls how many underlying training samples are needed for latent-feature recovery. We distinguish static masking , where each sample is assigned a single random mask that is reused throughout training, from dynamic masking , commonly used in practice [ 27 , 38 ] , in which the mask is independently resampled each time a sample is used during pretraining. More generally, assigning each sample K K independent masks and reusing them thereafter interpolates between these two regimes at fixed number of underlying samples. This allows us to isolate mask diversity from data diversity. Our analysis predicts that increasing K K lowers the recovery threshold, with corresponding improvements in downstream performance in the settings studied. This prediction prompted us to revisit how the contribution of mask diversity is assessed empirically. In language modeling, dynamic masking has been reported to provide only modest gains over reusing a fixed collection of masks [ 38 ] , but their static baseline already uses K = 10 K=10 pre-generated masks per sequence rather than a single fixed mask. Data2Vec 2.0 shows substantial improvements in image classification accuracy by increasing the number of masked views per sample within each training update [ 5 ] . Furthermore, in vision, self-supervised image learning commonly uses random cropping, flipping, and color transformations to generate changing views of the same sample [ 18 , 50 ] . In MAE specifically, standard pretraining combines random cropping and flipping with mask resampling [ 27 ] . Under a newly drawn crop, for example, the same patch mask can hide different content from the original image. We therefore hypothesize that stochastic image augmentation adds another source of prediction-task diversity, obscuring the effect of resampling the mask itself. Guided by this hypothesis, we compare static and dynamic masking with and without stochastic cropping and flipping . Without these transformations, dynamic masking improves downstream accuracy in CNN autoencoders on CIFAR-10 and ViT-Base on ImageNet-100 ( Fig. 1 (b,c)). In the ViT experiments, reintroducing cropping and flipping substantially narrows the observed static–dynamic gap, mainly because static masking improves ( Fig. 5 ). Finite- K K experiments further show progressive improvements as each image is exposed to more masks ( Fig. 4 ). A complementary BERT-Medium pilot finds improvements with increasing mask diversity on GLUE tasks, extending the qualitative evidence beyond vision ( Sec. 5 ). Together, these results distinguish two benefits of masked representation learning: the prediction objective can favor useful correlations over nuisance variance, while renewing the masks can lower the sample complexity required to learn those correlations. By identifying this distinction, the theory motivates a controlled test of its relevance beyond the solvable model. The main contributions of this paper are the following: • Under suitable heterogeneous noise, we prove that a linear masked autoencoder recovers the latent direction for all sufficiently large finite sample complexity α = n / d \alpha=n/d , whereas unmasked linear reconstruction (PCA) fails for every fixed α > 0 \alpha>0 . Replica calculations complement this guarantee by predicting the recovery threshold ( Sec. 3 ). • We formulate a tractable high-dimensional model of a two-stage learning protocol: self-supervised learning (SSL) through masked reconstruction, followed by supervised linear probing with a frozen encoder ( Sec. 2 ). For linear and nonlinear autoencoders, we derive replica predictions for feature recovery and downstream accuracy as functions of the masking ratio and mask diversity, showing the benefit of resampling the masks ( Sec. 4 ). • Guided by our theoretical predictions, we test the role of mask diversity in vision and language. Dynamic masking improves downstream performance without stochastic cropping and flipping; adding these transformations substantially narrows the observed static–dynamic gap in the ViT setting, consistent with overlapping sources of prediction-task diversity. A BERT-Medium pilot provides complementary evidence for the benefit of mask diversity in language modeling ( Sec. 5 ).

sections.heading: Further related work
sections.text: We outline the broad lines of related work here; App. A provides an expanded comparison with the closest references and clarifies the differences in setting, analytical scope, and contribution.

sections.heading: Statistical-physics theory of neural networks.
sections.text: Our replica analysis builds on high-dimensional empirical risk minimization [ 4 , 40 , 21 ] , shallow-autoencoder dynamics [ 47 ] , and denoising autoencoders [ 20 ] . Conde Mendes et al. [19] prove an advantage of nonlinear autoencoders over PCA. Heterogeneous noise has also been studied in supervised learning [ 3 , 2 ] .

sections.heading: Theory of masked learning.
sections.text: Existing work connects masked autoencoding to contrastive learning and downstream guarantees [ 60 ] , and establishes latent identifiability in hierarchical models [ 33 ] . Bisulco et al. [13] characterize linear MAEs with full reconstruction from masked inputs, including visible coordinates rather than only hidden targets. Their analysis relates patch size and masking ratio to the spatial correlations learned. Dong et al. [24] analyze decoupled coordinate predictors through rigorous ridgeless-regression risk formulas, accounting for both corrupted covariates and the samples supplying a selected prediction target. Single-coordinate prediction also connects to factored attention [ 48 ] . Wortsman Zurich et al. [55] characterize a spiked-model recovery transition in the joint matrix of single-coordinate ridge predictors and establish prediction-risk advantages over PCA in structured covariance settings. Cabannes et al. [16] distinguish sample variability from augmentation variability in SSL generalization bounds; additional views can reduce the latter without removing the former.

sections.heading: Spiked models and heteroskedastic noise.
sections.text: Our linear baseline connects to spiked covariance models [ 31 ] and PCA recovery transitions [ 8 , 12 ] . Hong et al. [28] characterize PCA under heteroskedastic noise. Spectral methods addressing heteroskedasticity include weighted PCA [ 29 ] , diagonal correction through HeteroPCA [ 59 ] , and optimal estimators for doubly heteroskedastic noise [ 61 ] . We study how masking changes the reconstruction objective to promote recovery, without supplying the coordinate variances or their distribution.

sections.heading: Data and noise heterogeneity.
sections.text: Our goal is to compare prediction objectives and masking protocols for a data distribution that enables sharp high-dimensional analysis. Inspired by insights into the advantage of masking from [ 9 ] and by work on unsupervised learning in high dimensions [ 31 , 22 , 37 ] , we consider a data model that separates a shared informative feature in the form of a spike from coordinate-specific nuisance fluctuations. Concretely, we consider n n samples with d d coordinates generated as x μ ​ i = β d ​ λ μ ​ u i ⋆ + γ i ⋆ ​ z μ ​ i , μ ∈ [ n ] , i ∈ [ d ] . x_{\mu i}=\sqrt{\frac{\beta}{d}}\,\lambda_{\mu}u_{i}^{\star}+\sqrt{\gamma_{i}^{\star}}\,z_{\mu i},\qquad\mu\in[n],\quad i\in[d]. (1) Here 𝒖 ⋆ \bm{u}^{\star} is the shared latent direction (spike), λ μ \lambda_{\mu} is the latent variable of sample μ \mu , and β > 0 \beta>0 controls signal strength. The variance γ i ⋆ \gamma_{i}^{\star} sets the strength of nuisance fluctuations in coordinate i i : a large value increases input variance independently of the spiked direction. These variances are drawn once and shared by all samples, whereas the noise realizations z μ ​ i z_{\mu i} change across samples and coordinates. The variables λ μ \lambda_{\mu} and u i ⋆ u_{i}^{\star} are independently drawn from centered, unit-second-moment distributions P λ P_{\lambda} and P u P_{u} ; z μ ​ i ∼ iid 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) z_{\mu i}\mathrel{\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,1) , and the variances γ i ⋆ ∼ iid P γ \gamma_{i}^{\star}\mathrel{\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}}P_{\gamma} are positive. sections.heading: Static, finite- K K , and dynamic masking.
sections.text: The choice K = 1 K=1 gives static masking . Increasing K K adds masked views without adding underlying samples. At a fixed dataset, the average over masks converges to the mask expectation as K → ∞ K\to\infty . We refer to this loss as the dynamic masking objective; drawing a fresh mask at each encounter provides stochastic evaluations of it. The high-dimensional analysis takes n , d → ∞ n,d\to\infty at fixed K K and obtains dynamic masking as K → ∞ K\rightarrow\infty ( Sec. B.2.4 ). Our two-stage protocol first learns a representation from unlabeled data and then fits a supervised probe with the encoder frozen. We assess both whether pretraining recovers the shared latent direction and whether the resulting representation supports prediction from a small, independent labeled dataset.

sections.heading: Downstream task and linear probing.
Analytical predictions and optimality.
sections.text: The replica method predicts feature recovery after pretraining and the accuracy of the subsequent frozen-representation probe ( Secs. C.1 and C.2 ). Replica calculations predict weak recovery thresholds by locating where an uninformative solution becomes unstable to a small alignment. These predictions concern continuous recovery transitions and are validated with simulations; an earlier discontinuous transition requires a separate analysis ( Sec. D.2.1 ). Below, “weak recovery threshold” has this predictive meaning when referring to replica results. Independently, Sec. 3 proves a separation between masked linear autoencoder and PCA. We also compare feature recovery with a matched Bayes-optimal reference that uses the same unlabeled samples but is supplied with the latent priors and realized coordinate variances. Unmasked reconstruction and finite- K K comparisons isolate the effects of the objective and mask reuse, respectively; the Bayes reference instead assesses the gap to matched inference with additional prior information. Following Lesieur et al. [37] , App. F gives the state evolution and heteroskedastic approximate message passing (AMP) updates. Downstream evaluation uses the same scalar logistic probe for AMP and the autoencoders ( Sec. G.2 ).

sections.heading: 3 A provable advantage of masked reconstruction
sections.text: We first isolate the effect of the prediction objective. Unmasked autoencoders learn a compressed representation by reconstructing the full input through a low-dimensional bottleneck. The bottleneck forces the learner to select which variations in the data to preserve, with reconstruction error providing the criterion for this selection. Unmasked reconstruction is therefore a natural baseline for asking whether the features most useful for reconstructing the input also capture its shared latent structure.

sections.text: For the masked objective ( 3 ), we likewise consider a linear activation, set λ R = 0 \lambda_{R}=0 , and average over masks. Write 𝒘 = d ​ Q ​ 𝒓 \bm{w}=\sqrt{dQ}\,\bm{r} , with Q ≥ 0 Q\geq 0 and ‖ 𝒓 ‖ = 1 \|\bm{r}\|=1 , and let Σ = diag ⁡ ( γ 1 ⋆ , … , γ d ⋆ ) + β ​ 𝒖 ⋆ ​ ( 𝒖 ⋆ ) ⊤ / d \Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\gamma_{1}^{\star},\ldots,\gamma_{d}^{\star})+\beta\bm{u}^{\star}(\bm{u}^{\star})^{\top}/d be the population covariance conditional on the planted direction and coordinate variances. Both population losses per sample are quadratic in Q Q . Their terms linear in Q Q are − 2 ​ Q -2Q times the following rewards: Unmasked: \displaystyle\text{Unmasked:} 𝒓 ⊤ Σ 𝒓 Masked: \displaystyle\bm{r}^{\top}\Sigma\bm{r}\qquad\text{Masked:}\quad ρ ⁡ ( 1 − ρ ) ​ 𝒓 ⊤ ​ ( Σ − diag ⁡ Σ ) ​ 𝒓 \displaystyle\rho(1-\rho)\,\bm{r}^{\top}\bigl(\Sigma-\operatorname{diag}\Sigma\bigr)\bm{r} (6) Unmasked reconstruction rewards total variance, whereas masked prediction rewards cross-correlations between different coordinates. The diagonal is absent from the masked reward because masking prevents a coordinate from predicting itself, removing the reward for its own variance: only correlations with visible coordinates can help reconstruct it. To illustrate this effect, consider a coordinate with large noise variance, preserving its fluctuations in the compressed representation can substantially reduce unmasked reconstruction error, even though those fluctuations carry no information about the shared structure (the spike 𝒖 ⋆ \bm{u}^{\star} in our model). But when that coordinate is hidden, its independent noise cannot be predicted from the visible coordinates. The shared feature 𝒖 ⋆ \bm{u}^{\star} , by contrast, creates correlations between visible and hidden coordinates and can therefore improve masked prediction. Noise no longer earns a direct reward through its variance, and the quadratic prediction penalty discourages reliance on noisy inputs. Together, these effects can allow masked reconstruction to favor cleaner coordinates. The full loss decomposition is given in Secs. E.1.4 and E.1.5 .

sections.heading: Interpreting the separation.
sections.text: Fig. 2 (b,c) illustrates how heterogeneity changes the comparison with the homogeneous reference: masking recovers while PCA can remain uninformative 3 3 3 Sec. H.2 shows that the positive cosine similarity of PCA in Fig. 2 (b) is due to finite-size effects. . The bounded example (panel b) shows that this effect does not require arbitrarily large coordinate variances; the signal can remain below the noise spectral edge even when the variance support is compact. With unbounded support (panel c), extreme coordinate variances instead drive the leading sample component away from the shared feature. The respective PCA arguments are given in Secs. E.1.3 and E.1.2 . The masked reward in ( 6 ) involves the same off-diagonal covariance structure used by diagonal-deletion PCA [ 25 ] , but the full masked objective also contains a noise-sensitive, direction-dependent prediction penalty. In our simulations, dynamic masking achieves better alignment than both diagonal-deletion PCA and HeteroPCA ( Sec. H.4 ). The theorem guarantees recovery for all sufficiently large finite α \alpha for dynamic masking, but does not locate the sharp transition, for which the replica analysis provides a prediction. Having established why the masked objective can favor useful structure, we next ask how its performance changes when each sample supplies only a finite collection of masks.

sections.heading: 4 Mask diversity and sample complexity
sections.text: We now keep the original dataset fixed and vary the number K K of masks per sample. Reusing a fixed collection of masks repeatedly presents the same visible-to-hidden prediction tasks; increasing K K adds new tasks without adding independent observations. The question is how this change affects the weak recovery thresholds and downstream performance. Figure 3: Replica predictions track learning across mask diversity. Colors distinguish K = K= 1 1 (static) , 2 , 4 ,2,4 and the dynamic masking limit. Solid curves are replica predictions and markers are finite-dimensional simulations. Green curves show the Bayes-optimal pretraining reference, evaluated with the same logistic probe for the lower row; green diamonds show AMP results ( Secs. F.5 and H.14 ). Error bars show ± 1 \pm 1 SD. See App. H for experimental details.

sections.heading: Predicting learning across mask diversity.
sections.text: Our replica analysis yields high-dimensional learning curves for static , finite- K K , and dynamic masking , resolving their dependence on sample complexity α \alpha , masking ratio ρ \rho , and activation function ( Sec. C.1 ). It predicts alignment with the planted feature and the effective noise along the learned direction; the downstream analysis then translates these quantities into classification accuracy under the linear-probe protocol introduced in Sec. 2 . Fig. 3 compares these predictions with numerical training at finite dimension. Across the tested activations, increasing mask diversity K K lowers the weak recovery threshold and improves alignment above the transition in the settings shown. The replica predictions capture not only these threshold shifts, but also the magnitude and α \alpha -dependence of the cosine similarity over the displayed range. The theory also captures training and test errors ( Fig. 10 ). Thus the analysis quantifies how mask resampling changes the representation learned from a given number of examples.

sections.heading: From feature recovery to downstream performance.
sections.text: The lower row of Fig. 3 shows how these representation gains translate into classification accuracy. The linear-probe predictions ( Sec. G.2 ) track the numerical results as sample complexity and mask diversity vary across the four activation functions. Together, the two rows show that the theory captures both latent-feature recovery during pretraining and the downstream usefulness of the frozen representation. The Bayes-optimal pretraining curve provides the reference using the matched priors and the realized coordinate variances ( App. F ). Increasing mask diversity brings the representations closer to this reference in the displayed comparisons, while a gap can remain even with dynamic masking ( Fig. 3 ).

Increasing K K improves accuracy in the settings shown, and the curves approach the dynamic masking reference. The number of training samples is held fixed. Bars and shading show ± 1 \pm 1 SD across seeds; see App. H for details. The derivation and conditions underlying this expansion are given in Secs. D.2 and D.2.1 . The prefactor κ 2 / β 2 \kappa_{2}/\beta^{2} sets the weak-signal scale, including the cost of variance heterogeneity. At leading order, mask diversity lowers the excess threshold by a term proportional to 1 / K 1/K : doubling K K halves this excess sample requirement, with smaller absolute gains at each doubling. This leading law is shared by linear, tanh, and ELU activations; ReLU has a different coefficient but retains the same ordering in K K ( Sec. D.2 ). Beyond weak signal, Fig. 18 compares linear threshold ratios computed from the full replica equations with the asymptotic prediction. The ratios continue to decrease with K K at the finite β \beta , even when they depart from the weak-signal expression. Finite-dimensional training in Fig. 3 supports this predicted ordering across all four activations.

sections.heading: Mask diversity can change the learning mechanism.
sections.text: Beyond the weak-signal expansion, replicas reveal a qualitative difference between static and dynamic masking. In the linear case, at the weak recovery transition, static masking does not preferentially use cleaner coordinates to identify the feature: its threshold reflects noise heterogeneity only through the aggregate moment κ 2 \kappa_{2} . Dynamic masking can instead find and favor cleaner coordinates as recovery begins, implicitly learning which coordinates provide more reliable information. At suitable masking ratios, this adaptation provides an additional benefit not captured by the leading weak-signal law ( 7 ). Sec. D.4 derives this distinction and compares noise distributions with identical static but different dynamic thresholds.

sections.heading: Interaction with the masking ratio.
sections.text: The finite- K K penalty in ( 7 ) is smallest at balanced masking and grows towards either endpoint. Near these extremes, each view offers relatively few visible or hidden coordinates, and a small collection of masks provides few distinct prediction tasks. Increasing K K reduces this penalty. The shallow-model sweep in Fig. 4 (a) illustrates the associated improvement in accuracy and the broader range of useful masking ratios as K K increases. At finite signal strength, the best downstream masking ratio also depends on the activation and the learned representation’s noise, so it need not minimize the leading threshold alone.

sections.heading: Isolating mask resampling.
sections.text: We test the qualitative mask-diversity prediction in CNN autoencoders on CIFAR-10 and ViT-Base on ImageNet-100. Without stochastic cropping or flipping during pretraining, dynamic masking improves downstream accuracy over static masking in both architectures ( Fig. 1 (b,c)); see Fig. 7 for ViT top-1 accuracy. At suitable masking ratios, resampling alone reaches accuracy comparable to our reference combining dynamic masking with random cropping and flipping [ 27 ] . With extended pretraining and probing schedules, dynamic masking (without stochastic cropping or flipping) reaches accuracy comparable to the ImageNet-100 MAE baseline reported by Zhang et al. [60] ( Tables 3 and 4 ).

sections.heading: Interaction with cropping and flipping.
sections.text: Fig. 5 compares static and dynamic ViT masking with and without cropping and flipping. Under static masking , patch positions remain fixed while transformations change the visible content and reconstruction targets. Cropping and flipping substantially improve static masking, narrowing the gap to dynamic masking. Fig. 14 extends the comparison to our CNN experiments with CIFAR-10 leading to the same qualitative conclusions.

sections.heading: Finite mask diversity.
sections.text: In the CNN sweep of Fig. 4 (b), each image is assigned K K independently drawn masks that are reused throughout pretraining, whereas dynamic masking draws a fresh mask at every presentation. For validation-selected encoders, mean downstream accuracy generally increases with K K , approaching the dynamic-masking reference while using the same pretraining images. To assess sensitivity to the training protocol, we repeat the comparison at ρ = 0.625 \rho=0.625 with five paired seeds and a fixed learning rate under a schedule defined in optimizer updates. The mask-diversity trend persists both with validation-selected checkpoints and when all encoders are evaluated at the same 125k-update checkpoint ( Sec. H.10 ). For unmasked reconstruction in Fig. 1 , we found that lower reconstruction error need not imply better representations for the downstream task: continued pretraining can reduce reconstruction MSE while linear probing degrades ( Figs. 12 and 13 ).

sections.heading: Mask diversity in language modeling.
sections.text: A BERT-Medium pilot compares K = 1 K=1 , K = 10 K=10 , and dynamic masking , using only [MASK] replacements ( Table 1 ). The corpus, architecture, and pretraining budget are shared across masking conditions. The ordering dynamic masking > K = 10 > K = 1 >K=10>K=1 holds in mean development score on seven of the eight GLUE tasks. Additional results and experimental details are provided in Sec. H.13 .

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: Our analysis separates two benefits of masked learning: masked prediction can favor shared structure over nuisance variance, while mask resampling can reduce the sample complexity required to recover that structure. We establish the first benefit rigorously in the linear model and quantify the second through replica calculations that agree with simulations. The CNN and ViT experiments, together with the BERT pilot, support the relevance of mask diversity across architectures and data modalities. This perspective connects masked reconstruction to theories of data augmentation. Analyses based on transformation groups explain statistical gains through invariance and averaging [ 17 , 41 ] ; in joint-embedding self-supervised learning, multiple views can reduce augmentation variability while retaining the variability associated with the original observations [ 16 ] . Our analysis gives a complementary account for masked reconstruction: changing K K preserves both the underlying dataset and the distribution of individual masks, yet changes the predicted recovery threshold. The weak-signal law quantifies the additional sample requirement at finite K K and the diminishing gains from increasing mask diversity. The ViT comparison suggests that geometric augmentation can partly compensate for mask reuse. A predictive theory of augmentation should therefore explain when geometric transformations and mask resampling offer complementary benefits, and when one reduces the benefit of the other. Our replica analysis also identifies a qualitative change in learning: dynamic masking can exploit cleaner coordinates at the recovery transition, while static masking lacks this adaptation. Whether resampling similarly changes which information is learned in larger models remains an open question. Better representations need not require more data; they can come from a greater diversity of prediction tasks on the same observations.

sections.heading: Appendix A Detailed comparison with the closest prior work
sections.text: The main text outlines the broad lines of related work. Here we expand on the closest references to clarify both their settings and what their analyses establish. We compare data models, prediction objectives, and masking protocols, as well as the observables and guarantees studied. These distinctions locate our contributions: recovery under heterogeneous noise for the exact mask-averaged objective, and replica predictions for mask diversity and downstream performance.

sections.heading: Reconstruction and useful features.
sections.text: The reconstruction–perception mismatch identified by Balestriero and LeCun [9] motivates our separation: a direction can explain substantial input variance without carrying useful latent information. Their closed-form linear denoising analysis shows how corruption, including masking, can improve this alignment. In our spiked model, coordinate-dependent noise makes the obstruction explicit, and hidden-target prediction admits a recovery guarantee at linear sample complexity: every global minimizer of the exact mask-averaged linear objective weakly recovers at linear sample complexity while ordinary PCA fails ( Theorem 3.1 ).

sections.heading: Full reconstruction from masked inputs.
sections.text: The linear MAE analyzed by Bisulco et al. [13] has untied encoder and decoder matrices, whereas our bottleneck uses tied weights. More crucially, their mask-averaged analytical loss reconstructs all coordinates from masked inputs, including visible coordinates; ours scores only hidden targets. The visible-coordinate rewards retain a contribution from reproducing input variance, changing both the loss landscape and its masking-ratio dependence. Their characterization of critical points and of the spatial correlations selected by patch size and masking ratio is therefore closely relevant, but its spectral solution does not directly solve our objective. Our statistical analysis follows how the structure favored by hidden-target prediction translates into recovery at finite sample size and under finite mask reuse. These are different objectives and constraints, rather than a general performance ordering.

sections.heading: Single-token prediction and factored attention.
sections.text: Rende et al. [48] connect factored attention to generalized Potts conditionals and use replicas to predict generalization in a Gaussian relaxation. There, predicting one coordinate from all the others probes a full-rank random precision matrix. This differs from our low-rank signal with diagonal heterogeneous noise both in correlation structure and in the number of targets per mask: a positive limiting fraction is hidden in our model. The shared tied bottleneck couples these prediction tasks, so its alignment with the planted feature, and the downstream utility of that alignment, become explicit observables as the number of reused masks varies.

sections.heading: The joint matrix of single-coordinate predictors.
sections.text: Single-coordinate prediction can itself reveal latent structure: Wortsman Zurich et al. [55] analyze the joint matrix of self-supervised ridge predictors, rigorously characterizing its spectrum, prediction risk, and spiked-model BBP recovery transition. They also establish prediction-risk advantages over PCA in structured covariance settings. Coupling an extensive set of hidden targets through a shared tied bottleneck changes the estimator in our work; mask diversity is an additional statistical control. Our analysis follows its effects on recovery and downstream performance via replicas, alongside a rigorous recovery separation under heteroskedastic noise for the exact mask-averaged objective. Nevertheless, it is important to stress that recovering latent structure through the data correlations exploited by masked prediction is already established in their work.

sections.heading: Masking ratio and a selected prediction target.
sections.text: Dong et al. [24] start from a loss over all hidden coordinates, but decouple their linear predictors and solve a stylized regression for one selected target, y = X ​ 𝜷 + ϵ y=X\bm{\beta}+\epsilon in their notation. Their isotropic and spiked covariance assumptions describe the remaining covariates X X ; the target coefficient and residual noise are specified separately. Consequently, this target need not be statistically representative of the other coordinates of the augmented sample ( X , y ) (X,y) . The resulting risk formulas rigorously quantify how masking both corrupts covariates and selects the samples supplying this target. In our common-factor model, every coordinate follows the same generative construction without a designated response, and all hidden targets train the same tied bottleneck; the analysis then follows collective feature recovery. Their fixed-ratio theory motivates randomized masking ratios, with downstream benefits assessed across modalities; our finite-reuse calculation keeps the ratio fixed and links representation alignment to a finite-label probe, with replica rather than rigorous guarantees for the general learning curves.

sections.heading: Contrastive connections and downstream guarantees.
sections.text: The connection between masked reconstruction and useful representations is also explicit in Zhang et al. [60] : reconstruction induces alignment on a mask-based augmentation graph, supporting downstream guarantees and an analysis of masking ratio and dimensional collapse. Our recovery thresholds address a more specific statistical question: how reusing a finite collection of masks changes the learned alignment at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio. The downstream calculation then tracks the effect of that alignment on a probe trained with finitely many labels.

sections.heading: Identifiability in hierarchical models.
sections.text: Under the hierarchical generative and invertibility assumptions of Kong et al. [33] , masking ratio and patch size determine which latent variables are shared between visible and hidden regions and can be identified. In our additive-noise model, the relevant observable is partial alignment with a planted direction at finite sample-to-dimension ratio. The recovery transition and its dependence on mask diversity concern statistical estimation under these different data and encoder assumptions, rather than an alternative identifiability statement for their hierarchy.

sections.heading: Nonlinear recovery beyond PCA.
sections.text: Conde Mendes et al. [19] show that nonlinear autoencoders recover higher-order structure invisible to PCA, and that reconstruction loss can misalign with representation quality. Our signal is covariance-visible, but heterogeneous variances obstruct ordinary PCA. Hidden-target prediction changes which covariance structure the objective rewards, yielding a separation that does not require nonlinearity. Complementary high-dimensional work studies how pretraining sample size and representation dimensionality jointly control downstream linear-probe generalization in spiked models [ 44 ] .

sections.heading: Noise-aware spectral alternatives.
sections.text: HeteroPCA [ 59 ] and whitening-based methods [ 35 ] address the same nuisance of heterogeneous noise through spectral correction. Fig. 8 compares such estimators on the same observations: our separation from ordinary PCA does not imply a separation from all spectral methods. The comparison locates masking among several routes to recovery. It changes which structure the reconstruction objective rewards, without supplying the autoencoder with the coordinate variances or their distribution.

sections.heading: Bayes-optimal inference and the role of prior information.
sections.text: Our Bayes analysis builds on the low-rank matrix-estimation framework of Lesieur et al. [36] , Lesieur et al. [37] , which connects matched priors and output channels to approximate message passing and state evolution. We specialize this framework to coordinate-dependent Gaussian noise to obtain the reference learning curves and AMP updates in App. F . For Gaussian latent priors, the continuous recovery threshold is α c BO = [ β 2 ​ 𝔼 γ ​ ( γ − 2 ) ] − 1 \alpha_{c}^{\rm BO}=[\beta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}(\gamma^{-2})]^{-1} when the inverse second moment is finite ( Sec. F.8 ). Its dependence on inverse variances highlights the information available in low-noise coordinates. Zhang and Mondelli [61] provide an independent rigorous foundation: their analysis of doubly heteroskedastic matrix denoising yields this weak-estimation threshold under their Gaussian-prior and compact, positive covariance-support assumptions, and a covariance-aware spectral estimator attains it under their additional technical condition. Thus the Bayes reference connects our reconstruction-based learners to an established optimal-inference benchmark, rather than introducing a new information-theoretic limit. The distinction in available information matters for interpreting the comparison. Our Bayes reference uses the matched latent priors and the realized coordinate variances, whereas the autoencoders receive neither the variances nor their distribution. A remaining gap to Bayes therefore reflects both the reconstruction objective and the additional information used by matched inference. Increasing mask diversity improves how that objective uses the observations; it does not supply the learner with the noise model. The variance-consistency calculation in App. F discusses learning the noise levels from the samples, separately from the known-variance benchmark used here.

sections.heading: Augmentation multiplicity and finite reuse.
sections.text: Prior work has studied the benefit of drawing multiple augmented views of the same example. Fort et al. [26] show empirically that averaging several freshly sampled augmentations per image can improve supervised generalization, while Cabannes et al. [16] analyze the corresponding multi-view setting theoretically and separate variability due to sampling original examples from variability due to sampling their augmentations. These works vary the number of views used for an example while preserving the underlying augmentation distribution. We study a different axis: finite reuse . Each training sample is assigned K K masks that are held fixed throughout learning, so changing K K changes the finite collection of prediction tasks available to the learner rather than the number of views averaged within an update. Replica predictions quantify how this finite mask diversity changes feature recovery and downstream accuracy, including the weak-signal excess sample requirement in ( 7 ). The masks contain no additional information about the planted feature; we show that their benefit comes from how a richer collection of prediction tasks allows the objective to extract information already present in the observed samples.

sections.heading: Mask resampling and other augmentations.
sections.text: Dynamic masking in RoBERTa [ 38 ] and multiple masked views per update in data2vec 2.0 [ 5 ] already exploit variation in prediction tasks. The interaction with image augmentation matters when interpreting its benefit: even fixed patch positions expose changing content under stochastic cropping and flipping. Our vision comparisons isolate this interaction, while the BERT pilot provides complementary evidence for finite mask diversity. Group-based accounts of augmentation through invariance and averaging [ 17 , 41 ] offer another perspective; here the controlled variable is the reuse of prediction tasks from each original observation. These experiments test the qualitative role of mask diversity beyond the solvable model, without assuming that its quantitative recovery law transfers to these architectures and datasets.

sections.heading: Why allow unequal noise variances?
sections.text: The distinction between variance and task-relevant information motivates the model. Reconstruction objectives can emphasize components that are weakly useful for perception [ 9 ] . Examples of nuisance variation dominating leading components include illumination in face recognition [ 11 ] , natural-image backgrounds superimposed on handwritten digits [ 1 ] , and heterogeneous noise in biological data [ 15 ] . These examples motivate separating useful structure from variance; they do not identify their covariance structure with the coordinate-noise model studied here. Our model isolates this distinction using a single shared feature and independently varying coordinate noise levels. The training samples 𝒙 μ ∈ ℝ d \bm{x}_{\mu}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are generated from the heteroskedastic rank-one model x μ ​ i = β d λ μ u i ⋆ + γ i ⋆ z μ ​ i , μ = 1 , … , n , i = 1 , … , d . x_{\mu i}=\sqrt{\frac{\beta}{d}}\,\lambda_{\mu}u_{i}^{\star}+\sqrt{\gamma_{i}^{\star}}\,z_{\mu i},\qquad\mu=1,\ldots,n,\quad i=1,\ldots,d. sections.text: It remains to connect the two specializations. For fixed positive integer s s , write 𝒉 s = ( h 1 , … , h s ) ⊤ , 𝜹 r = ( δ r 1 , … , δ r s ) ⊤ . \bm{h}_{s}=(h^{1},\ldots,h^{s})^{\top},\qquad\bm{\delta}_{r}=(\delta_{r}^{1},\ldots,\delta_{r}^{s})^{\top}. The components of a fixed 𝜹 r \bm{\delta}_{r} are generally correlated across replicas, but the fluctuation vectors are i.i.d. across the mask index r r . Define q 𝖺 ​ ( h , δ ) := ρ ​ Q I 𝖺𝖺 ​ σ ​ ( ( 1 − ρ ) ​ h + δ ) 2 − 2 ​ σ ​ ( ( 1 − ρ ) ​ h + δ ) ​ ( ρ ​ h − δ ) . q_{\mathsf{a}}(h,\delta):=\rho Q_{I}^{\mathsf{a}\mathsf{a}}\sigma\!\left((1-\rho)h+\delta\right)^{2}-2\sigma\!\left((1-\rho)h+\delta\right)(\rho h-\delta). (C.119) Conditioning on 𝒉 s \bm{h}_{s} and applying the law of large numbers across the independent mask index gives 1 K ​ ∑ r = 1 K ∑ 𝖺 = 1 s q 𝖺 ​ ( h 𝖺 , δ r 𝖺 ) → K → ∞ ∑ 𝖺 = 1 s 𝔼 δ 𝖺 ​ q 𝖺 ​ ( h 𝖺 , δ 𝖺 ) . \frac{1}{K}\sum_{r=1}^{K}\sum_{\mathsf{a}=1}^{s}q_{\mathsf{a}}\!\left(h^{\mathsf{a}},\delta_{r}^{\mathsf{a}}\right)\xrightarrow[K\to\infty]{}\sum_{\mathsf{a}=1}^{s}\mathbb{E}_{\delta^{\mathsf{a}}}q_{\mathsf{a}}\!\left(h^{\mathsf{a}},\delta^{\mathsf{a}}\right). (C.120) Only the marginal distribution of each replica component appears on the right-hand side. From ( C.117 ), δ 𝖺 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , ρ ⁡ ( 1 − ρ ) ​ Q Γ 𝖺𝖺 ) , \delta^{\mathsf{a}}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,\rho(1-\rho)Q_{\Gamma}^{\mathsf{a}\mathsf{a}}\right), (C.121) and therefore 𝔼 δ 𝖺 ​ q 𝖺 ​ ( h 𝖺 , δ 𝖺 ) = ℓ dyn ​ ( h 𝖺 , Q I 𝖺𝖺 , Q Γ 𝖺𝖺 ) . \mathbb{E}_{\delta^{\mathsf{a}}}q_{\mathsf{a}}\!\left(h^{\mathsf{a}},\delta^{\mathsf{a}}\right)=\ell_{\rm dyn}\!\left(h^{\mathsf{a}};Q_{I}^{\mathsf{a}\mathsf{a}},Q_{\Gamma}^{\mathsf{a}\mathsf{a}}\right). (C.123) This establishes the dynamic-mask limit directly inside the same generic replica framework. The sequential interpretation is therefore d , n → ∞ at fixed ​ K , generic replica reduction with ​ L = K + 1 , K → ∞ : Ψ K , out ( s ) ⟶ Ψ dyn , out ( s ) , followed by the usual replica continuation ​ s → 0 . \begin{gathered}d,n\to\infty\quad\text{at fixed }K,\\ \text{generic replica reduction with }L=K+1,\\ K\to\infty:\quad\Psi_{K,\mathrm{out}}^{(s)}\longrightarrow\Psi_{{\rm dyn},\mathrm{out}}^{(s)},\\ \text{followed by the usual replica continuation }s\to 0.\end{gathered} (C.124) Since the weight prior and the definitions of M M , Q I Q_{I} , and Q Γ Q_{\Gamma} are unchanged, the remainder of the saddle-point calculation is common to both finite- K K and dynamic masking; only the model-specific output functional changes.

sections.heading: C.2.4 Full-reconstruction autoencoder
sections.text: We derive the output channel for the full-reconstruction objective ( 5 ), in which both the encoder input and the reconstruction targets include all coordinates. For one sample, the reconstruction loss is ∑ i = 1 d [ x i − w i d ​ σ ​ ( h ) ] 2 , h = 1 d ​ ∑ i = 1 d w i ​ x i . \sum_{i=1}^{d}\left[x_{i}-\frac{w_{i}}{\sqrt{d}}\sigma(h)\right]^{2},\qquad h=\frac{1}{\sqrt{d}}\sum_{i=1}^{d}w_{i}x_{i}. (C.125) Dropping the term independent of 𝒘 \bm{w} gives the effective output loss ℓ full ​ ( h , Q I ) = Q I ​ σ ​ ( h ) 2 − 2 ​ h ​ σ ​ ( h ) . \ell_{\rm full}(h;Q_{I})=Q_{I}\sigma(h)^{2}-2h\sigma(h). (C.126) This is the full-reconstruction counterpart of the masked output loss ( B.23 ): the encoder and target fields are both h h , and the squared decoder norm is Q I Q_{I} rather than the masked fraction ρ ​ Q I \rho Q_{I} . In particular, the cross term is − 2 ​ h ​ σ ​ ( h ) -2h\sigma(h) instead of − 2 ​ h r , mask ​ σ ​ ( h r , vis ) -2h_{r,\mathrm{mask}}\sigma(h_{r,\mathrm{vis}}) , making explicit the difference between reconstructing a field from itself and predicting its hidden part from its visible part. The generic output channel therefore specializes to L = 1 , 𝒇 = h , 𝜿 = 1 , Ω = 1 . L=1,\qquad\bm{f}=h,\qquad\bm{\kappa}=1,\qquad\Omega=1. P_{{\rm full},\mathrm{out}}(h;Q_{I})=\exp\!\left\{-\eta_{\rm th}\ell_{\rm full}(h;Q_{I})\right\}. (C.128) Hence the replicated output contribution is Ψ full , out ( s ) := 𝔼 λ ​ 𝔼 𝒉 s | λ ​ [ ∏ 𝖺 = 1 s exp ⁡ { − η th ​ ℓ full ​ ( h 𝖺 , Q I 𝖺𝖺 ) } ] , \Psi_{{\rm full},\mathrm{out}}^{(s)}:=\mathbb{E}_{\lambda}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{h}_{s}\mid\lambda}\left[\prod_{\mathsf{a}=1}^{s}\exp\!\left\{-\eta_{\rm th}\ell_{\rm full}\!\left(h^{\mathsf{a}};Q_{I}^{\mathsf{a}\mathsf{a}}\right)\right\}\right], (C.129) where 𝒉 s | λ ∼ 𝒩 s ​ ( β ​ λ ​ 𝑴 s , 𝖰 Γ , s ) . \bm{h}_{s}\mid\lambda\sim\mathcal{N}_{s}\!\left(\sqrt{\beta}\lambda\bm{M}_{s},\mathsf{Q}_{\Gamma,s}\right). (C.130)

sections.heading: Appendix D Replica recovery predictions and the role of mask diversity
sections.text: This appendix explains how mask diversity changes the onset of feature recovery and how dynamic masking exploits heterogeneous coordinate noise. We derive the recovery criterion and its factorization in Sec. D.1 , obtain the weak-signal cost of mask reuse in Sec. D.2 , and examine its finite-signal behavior in Sec. H.11 . The linear theory then identifies the noise-adaptation mechanism in Sec. D.4 . These predictions complement the learning curves and simulation comparisons in Figs. 2 , 3 and 4 . We use the replica-symmetric equations of App. C at zero ridge; the onset calculation follows the growth of an infinitesimal feature overlap from the uninformative solution.

sections.heading: D.4 Mask diversity changes how the learner uses heterogeneous noise
sections.text: The weak-signal law in ( 7 ) describes an additional sample requirement caused by mask reuse. At finite signal strength, the replica equations reveal a further distinction: static and dynamic masking can use the coordinate noise profile differently when learning first becomes possible. Static masking has a noise-independent response to an emerging feature at its regular linear recovery transition. Dynamic masking can instead give cleaner coordinates a larger response, lowering the threshold through an adaptation that the static critical solution lacks. Thus the protocols differ not only in how many samples they require, but also in how they extract the feature from those samples. We develop this interpretation using the fixed-signal factorization in Sec. D.1.3 and the dynamic linear equations in Sec. D.3 . Throughout this subsection, σ ⁡ ( h ) = h \sigma(h)=h , λ R = 0 \lambda_{R}=0 , 𝔼 γ ​ γ = 1 \mathbb{E}_{\gamma}\gamma=1 , and κ 2 = 𝔼 γ ​ γ 2 < ∞ \kappa_{2}=\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}\gamma^{2}<\infty ; the concrete examples have finite positive variance support and Gaussian latent priors. We evaluate the response at the continuous recovery onset defined above.

sections.heading: D.4.1 Coordinate response separates noise adaptation from mask reuse
sections.text: The coordinate susceptibility v c ​ ( γ ) v_{c}(\gamma) describes the response to an infinitesimal informative field near recovery. In particular, the input equation gives m ⁡ ( γ ) = m ^ ​ v ​ ( γ ) m(\gamma)=\widehat{m}v(\gamma) , with the same m ^ \widehat{m} at every coordinate variance. Ratios of susceptibilities therefore determine where the emerging feature alignment is concentrated. Using ( D.33 ), for two variances 0 < γ 1 < γ 2 0<\gamma_{1}<\gamma_{2} , v c ​ ( γ 1 ) v c ​ ( γ 2 ) = 1 + τ c ​ γ 2 1 + τ c ​ γ 1 . \frac{v_{c}(\gamma_{1})}{v_{c}(\gamma_{2})}=\frac{1+\tau_{c}\gamma_{2}}{1+\tau_{c}\gamma_{1}}. (D.143) For τ c > 0 \tau_{c}>0 , this ratio exceeds one: the response favors cleaner coordinates. At τ c = 0 \tau_{c}=0 it is uniform, while negative τ c \tau_{c} favors noisier coordinates on its admissible domain. This is a statement about the response to the shared feature, not equality or ordering of the realized coordinate weights. The noise levels are not supplied to the autoencoder; their influence on the response emerges from the reconstruction objective and the data. The general finite- K K factorization ( D.34 ) separates two contributions: η K , c 2 \eta_{K,c}^{2} measures output efficiency, while ℛ γ ​ ( τ K , c ) \mathcal{R}_{\gamma}(\tau_{K,c}) measures how coordinate reweighting changes the effective noise burden. Both depend on mask diversity through the full equations. The static and dynamic endpoints below show how the response itself changes, beyond the sample penalty captured by the weak-signal law.

sections.text: This subsection establishes the PCA obstructions and bounded-noise masking recovery used in Theorem 3.1 ; Sec. E.2 extends masking recovery beyond bounded variance support. The PCA statements concern the leading empirical principal component. The masking statements concern every global minimizer of the exact mask-averaged objective, with no replica assumption and no claim about convergence of a particular optimization algorithm. sections.heading: Appendix H Experimental settings and reporting
sections.text: We report the settings needed to interpret the comparisons below. Source code and per-run configurations are provided in the accompanying code and data supplement. In all figures, error bars and shaded bands indicate ± 1 \pm 1 sample standard deviation (SD) across seeds around the empirical mean for each condition. Single-run results are shown without error bars.

sections.heading: Mask diversity and training budget.
sections.text: For finite K K , each example has K K independently drawn masks, fixed throughout pretraining. Static masking is K = 1 K=1 ; dynamic masking draws fresh masks on repeated presentations. The number of underlying examples is unchanged. In the shallow experiments, each update averages over the fixed mask collection, or uses one fresh mask for dynamic training ( Sec. H.12 ). The CNN training schedule is specified below.

sections.heading: CNN data and evaluation.
sections.text: Fig. 1 (b) and Fig. 4 (b) use CIFAR-10 [ 34 ] with five independent encoder-initialization and data-split seeds. Each seed uses a balanced 40,000 40{,}000 -image training subset for both pretraining and labeled frozen probing. Masked pretraining and linear probing use 10,000 10{,}000 held-out images for validation. The separate official 10,000 10{,}000 -image test set supplies final accuracy. One probe is fitted per encoder; points report mean test accuracy and bars show ± 1 \pm 1 SD across the five seeds. The masked comparisons share the split and initialization within each seed.

sections.heading: CNN architecture and preprocessing.
sections.text: All CNN conditions use the same 854,563 854{,}563 -parameter autoencoder. Images are scaled to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] and standardized using channel statistics from the pretraining subset. The encoder receives the three masked image channels and a binary mask channel, with hidden pixels set to zero after standardization. Its four convolutions have output widths ( 32 , 64 , 128 , 128 ) (32,64,128,128) , kernel sizes ( 3 , 4 , 4 , 4 ) (3,4,4,4) , strides ( 1 , 2 , 2 , 2 ) (1,2,2,2) , padding one, and ReLU activations. The decoder uses three stride-two, kernel-four transposed convolutions with widths ( 128 , 64 , 32 ) (128,64,32) , padding one and ReLU, followed by a kernel-three, padding-one convolution to RGB. There are no skip connections or normalization layers. Global spatial averaging of the encoder’s 128 × 4 × 4 128\times 4\times 4 output gives the frozen representation. Images contain 64 64 nonoverlapping 4 × 4 4\times 4 patches; each mask hides round ⁡ ( 64 ​ ρ ) \operatorname{round}(64\rho) patches chosen uniformly without replacement.

sections.heading: CNN optimization.
sections.text: For the main CNN sweeps in Figs. 1 , 4 , 14 and 15 , we use AdamW [ 39 ] with batch size 512 512 , learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and gradient norm clipping at 5 5 . A validation-based plateau scheduler halves the learning rate, with patience five epochs and a minimum of 10 − 5 10^{-5} . For finite K K , each epoch traverses the fixed collection of 40,000 ​ K 40{,}000K image–mask pairs. Dynamic masking draws a fresh mask at every presentation throughout training. We group 32 32 presentations per image into one epoch for validation and scheduling, corresponding to 2,500 2{,}500 optimizer updates. Under dynamic masking, each image therefore receives 32 ​ E 32E independent mask draws over E E epochs. Validation uses one fixed mask per held-out image after each epoch. We retain the checkpoint with the lowest validation reconstruction MSE and stop after 15 15 epochs without improvement, with a minimum of 20 20 and a ceiling of 460 460 epochs. Under these parameters, our setting is always early-stopped and not undertrained.

sections.heading: CNN linear probes.
sections.text: Probes receive unmasked, unaugmented images and use the frozen 128 128 -dimensional representation, standardized coordinatewise using the probe training set. A linear ten-class head is fitted with cross-entropy, AdamW, batch size 512 512 , constant learning rate 10 − 2 10^{-2} , and zero weight decay. Classifier initialization and minibatch-shuffling seeds are fixed across encoders. The head with lowest validation cross-entropy is retained; training stops after 25 25 epochs without improvement, with a minimum of 20 20 and a ceiling of 200 200 epochs. All reported masked-model probes satisfy this stopping criterion. The unmasked checkpoint sweep uses the same probe settings with a 300 300 -epoch ceiling ( Sec. H.8 ).

sections.heading: ViT architecture and data.
sections.text: Our implementation adapts the U-MAE code of Zhang et al. [60] , which builds on MAE [ 27 ] . 4 4 4 U-MAE implementation: https://github.com/zhangq327/U-MAE . We use ViT-Base/16 on ImageNet-100, with 126,689 126{,}689 training and 5,000 5{,}000 validation images across 100 100 classes. Images have resolution 224 × 224 224\times 224 , yielding 196 196 patches. The encoder has 12 12 blocks, width 768 768 and 12 12 attention heads; the decoder has 8 8 blocks, width 512 512 and 16 16 heads, with MLP expansion ratio 4 4 throughout. Pretraining minimizes MSE on masked patches, using targets standardized within each patch. U-MAE’s uniformity penalty is disabled in all reported ViT runs; AdamW weight decay is retained. The inherited online classifier receives detached features and does not train the encoder. Reported accuracies use a separately fitted frozen probe.

sections.heading: ViT preprocessing and masking.
sections.text: Without stochastic cropping or flipping, images are resized bicubically to shorter side 256 256 and center-cropped to 224 × 224 224\times 224 . The augmented condition instead uses random resized crops with area fraction in [ 0.2 , 1 ] [0.2,1] and aspect ratio in [ 3 / 4 , 4 / 3 ] [3/4,4/3] , followed by horizontal flipping with probability 1 / 2 1/2 . Both conditions use ImageNet channel normalization. A random patch permutation retains ⌊ 196 ​ ( 1 − ρ ) ⌋ \lfloor 196(1-\rho)\rfloor visible patches. Static masking fixes this permutation per training image; dynamic masking redraws it at every presentation. With cropping and flipping, the static patch positions refer to the transformed image, whose content can change across epochs.

sections.heading: ViT pretraining.
sections.text: All masked runs in Fig. 1 (c) and Fig. 5 use 100 100 epochs of AdamW with momentum parameters ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (0.9,0.95) , weight decay 0.05 0.05 , peak learning rate 7.5 × 10 − 5 7.5\times 10^{-5} , ten warmup epochs and cosine decay to zero. The effective batch size is 128 128 : batches of 64 64 with two accumulation steps without cropping/flipping, and batches of 128 128 without accumulation in the augmented condition. Biases and normalization parameters are excluded from weight decay. We probe the final pretraining checkpoint. The comparison uses one common seed, with identical training and validation splits, initial autoencoder weights, optimizer settings, and pretraining budget across conditions. A separate frozen probe is fitted to each encoder using the same probe initialization and training and evaluation protocol. In contrast, the unaugmented curves in Fig. 1 (c) summarize three encoder initializations (seeds 0 , 1 , 2 0,1,2 ), with means and ± 1 \pm 1 SD.

sections.heading: ViT linear probes.
sections.text: The frozen encoder processes all patches. Its 768 768 -dimensional class-token representation feeds a non-affine batch-normalization layer and a linear 100 100 -class head. The head is trained with cross-entropy and LARS [ 57 ] , batch size 256 256 , momentum 0.9 0.9 , zero weight decay, peak learning rate 0.1 0.1 , ten warmup epochs and cosine decay to zero over 50 50 epochs. Probe training uses random resized crops with area fraction in [ 0.08 , 1 ] [0.08,1] , aspect ratio in [ 3 / 4 , 4 / 3 ] [3/4,4/3] , and horizontal flipping with probability 1 / 2 1/2 for every pretraining condition. Validation uses the deterministic resize and center crop above. Thus the no-cropping/no-flipping condition refers to pretraining. Probe seeds are fixed at zero, and we report validation top-5 accuracy at the final probe epoch. Unmasked checkpoint selection is described in Sec. H.8 . Table 4 ablates the use of stochastic augmentation during linear probing. We find that including or omitting stochastic augmentation yields quantitatively similar downstream performance.

sections.heading: Longer ViT training.
sections.text: The 100 100 -epoch protocol above is used to compare masking conditions under a common training budget. To assess the attainable absolute performance with the same architecture, we also adapt the longer training schedules of U-MAE and MAE [ 60 , 27 ] , retaining dynamic masking at ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 , no stochastic cropping or flipping during pretraining, and no uniformity penalty. Table 3 reports these checks, all using initialization zero and ImageNet-100 pretraining only. The 200 200 -epoch schedule uses effective batch 1024 1024 ( 128 × 8 128\times 8 accumulation), 40 40 warmup epochs and peak learning rate 6 × 10 − 4 6\times 10^{-4} . The longer MAE schedule uses effective batch 4096 4096 ( 64 × 64 64\times 64 accumulation), 40 40 warmup epochs and peak learning rate 2.4 × 10 − 3 2.4\times 10^{-3} ; it was stopped early, and the evaluated checkpoint is after 641 641 epochs of the planned 1600 1600 -epoch cosine schedule. Other pretraining settings remain as above. Each encoder is evaluated with the existing probe and with a 90 90 -epoch probe using effective batch 16,384 16{,}384 ( 512 × 32 512\times 32 accumulation), peak learning rate 6.4 6.4 and ten warmup epochs, following the MAE linear-probing recipe. Both probes use cropping and flipping. The larger batch is implemented by gradient accumulation; batch normalization uses the physical batch, and incomplete accumulation windows at the end of an epoch do not produce an optimizer update. With the 200 200 -epoch encoder, the longer probe reaches 61.50 % 61.50\% top-1 and 86.04 % 86.04\% top-5 accuracy without pretraining augmentation. For context, Zhang et al. [60] report 61.2 % 61.2\% and 67.5 % 67.5\% top-1 for MAE and regularized U-MAE, respectively, on ImageNet-100 with ViT-Base. These published results provide a reference under different training conditions. The additional runs show that the shorter protocol used for our masking comparisons does not exhaust the performance of the architecture; they vary the optimization schedule as well as batch size. See [ 5 ] for experiments showing the effect of the batch size on downstream performance. sections.text: We also repeat the 50 50 -epoch probes of the static and dynamic 100 100 -epoch encoders at ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 , using initialization zero and deterministic resize/center crop during probe training. All other probe settings and the pretrained checkpoints are held fixed. Their gap remains nearly unchanged ( 17.58 17.58 versus 17.78 17.78 points), indicating that probe augmentation does not account for the dynamic-masking advantage in this check. sections.heading: H.3 Top-1 accuracy for ViT
sections.text: Fig. 7 reports the top-1 counterparts of the ViT comparisons in Fig. 1 (c) and Fig. 5 , using the same pretrained encoders and frozen linear probes. The qualitative conclusions also hold for this metric: dynamic masking improves accuracy without cropping or flipping during pretraining, while these augmentations substantially improve static masking and narrow the gap to dynamic masking. Table 3 puts these absolute accuracies in context. At ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 , dynamic masking reaches 39.96 % 39.96\% top-1 under the main comparison protocol, increasing to 61.50 % 61.50\% and 59.12 % 59.12\% with the longer U-MAE and MAE schedules and 90 90 -epoch probes, respectively. All three settings use no cropping or flipping during pretraining. Thus, the shorter protocol used to compare masking conditions does not exhaust the architecture’s performance; these additional runs vary both the training schedule and batch size. Table 4 separately checks standard augmentation during linear probing. Removing probe cropping and flipping raises top-1 accuracy from 39.96 % 39.96\% to 41.98 % 41.98\% for dynamic masking and from 25.34 % 25.34\% to 26.22 % 26.22\% for static masking. The dynamic–static gap therefore persists ( 14.62 14.62 versus 15.76 15.76 percentage points), supporting the same conclusion with either probe protocol. Both tables report single-seed checks, distinct from the three-seed averages in Fig. 7 (a). Figure 7: The ViT masking comparison also holds for top-1 accuracy. sections.heading: H.4 Noise-aware spectral methods
sections.text: Fig. 8 adds diagonal-deletion PCA, HeteroPCA, and estimated-whitening PCA to the bounded and unbounded settings of Fig. 2 (b,c), with β = 1 \beta=1 and ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 for dynamic masking. Spectral estimators and autoencoders use d = 2000 d=2000 and 20 20 seeds; AMP uses d = 4000 d=4000 and ten seeds ( Sec. H.14 ). Bars show ± 1 \pm 1 SD. The added spectral methods use the same observations and seeds as ordinary PCA and receive neither the spike nor the true coordinate variances. Covariances are centered in the unbounded setting and uncentered in the bounded setting.

sections.heading: Spectral estimators.
sections.text: Write S = Σ ^ S=\widehat{\Sigma} the empirical covariance matrix, diag ⁡ ( S ) \operatorname{diag}(S) for its diagonal matrix, and off ⁡ ( S ) = S − diag ⁡ ( S ) \operatorname{off}(S)=S-\operatorname{diag}(S) . In this section we will work with the following additional spectral estimators: Diagonal-deletion PCA removes the empirical diagonal before spectral extraction, using off ⁡ ( S ) \operatorname{off}(S) . This baseline is studied alongside HeteroPCA by Zhang et al. [59] but was originally introduced by Florescu and Perkins [25] . We extract its largest-magnitude eigenpair, corresponding to a leading singular direction. This removes the direct diagonal noise contribution, but also discards the signal diagonal. Figure 8: Noise-aware spectral baselines for heteroskedastic noise. Cosine similarity versus sample complexity under (a) bounded and (b) unbounded heterogeneous noise. The comparison includes dynamic masking, unmasked reconstruction (ordinary PCA), diagonal-deletion PCA [ 25 ] , HeteroPCA [ 59 ] , estimated-whitening PCA [ 35 ] , and the Bayes-optimal baseline. Lines show theoretical references; markers show numerical estimates. Green curves give the Bayes-optimal state-evolution reference; green diamonds show AMP results ( Secs. F.5 and H.14 ). Bars show ± 1 \pm 1 SD; hollow AMP markers identify groups containing iteration-limited runs. HeteroPCA iteratively imputes the diagonal from a rank-one approximation while retaining the observed off-diagonal entries [ 59 , Algorithm 1] . We initialize with off ⁡ ( S ) \operatorname{off}(S) , retain the signed largest-magnitude eigenpair, and stop when the relative diagonal change is at most 10 − 8 10^{-8} . Unresolved runs are continued up to 10 5 10^{5} iterations; all 680 680 fits in the displayed comparison meet this criterion. Estimated-whitening PCA follows the noise-whitening approach of Leeb and Romanov [35] , who also discuss estimated noise covariances in Section 4.3. We estimate Γ ^ i ​ i = max ⁡ ( S i ​ i , 10 − 12 ) \widehat{\Gamma}_{ii}=\max(S_{ii},10^{-12}) and apply PCA to S W = Γ ^ − 1 / 2 S Γ ^ − 1 / 2 S_{\rm W}=\widehat{\Gamma}^{-1/2}S\widehat{\Gamma}^{-1/2} . If 𝒗 W \bm{v}_{\rm W} is its leading eigenvector, alignment is evaluated using Γ ^ 1 / 2 ​ 𝒗 W \widehat{\Gamma}^{1/2}\bm{v}_{\rm W} in the original coordinates. This baseline uses whitening and unwhitening without additional spectral shrinkage. Dynamic masking achieves higher mean alignment than diagonal-deletion PCA and HeteroPCA across both displayed sweeps, without explicit noise estimation or whitening. Neither the coordinate variances nor their distribution are supplied to the autoencoder: adaptation to heterogeneity emerges through the masked prediction objective ( Sec. D.4 ). This provides a complementary perspective to covariance-aware inference. For example, Zhang and Mondelli [61] construct spectral estimators using known noise covariances and signal strength, with optimality guarantees under their assumptions. Estimated-whitening PCA generally achieves higher alignment in our experiments and lies closer to the Bayes reference, using variances estimated from the same observations. The comparison therefore highlights the ability of masked prediction to learn informative structure without a separate procedure for estimating and correcting the noise.

sections.heading: The whitening-PCA threshold.
sections.text: The whitening threshold follows from the spiked-model analysis of Leeb and Romanov [35] . In our rank-one model with Gaussian latent priors, whitening by ( Γ ⋆ ) − 1 / 2 (\Gamma^{\star})^{-1/2} produces isotropic noise and a population signal eigenvalue ℓ W = β ∥ ( Γ ⋆ ) − 1 / 2 𝒖 ⋆ ∥ 2 / d → β 𝔼 γ [ γ − 1 ] \ell^{\rm W}=\beta\|(\Gamma^{\star})^{-1/2}\bm{u}^{\star}\|^{2}/d\to\beta\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}[\gamma^{-1}] . Their recovery condition is ℓ W > α − 1 / 2 \ell^{\rm W}>\alpha^{-1/2} , with the same onset after unwhitening, giving α c W = [ β 2 ​ 𝔼 γ ​ [ γ − 1 ] 2 ] − 1 \alpha_{c}^{\rm W}=[\beta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}[\gamma^{-1}]^{2}]^{-1} . Leeb and Romanov [35] also justify replacing the noise covariance by an estimate consistent in operator norm. For diagonal noise and a delocalized signal direction, they obtain such an estimate from the sample coordinate variances, as in the baseline above. Our bounded variance law and normalized Gaussian spike satisfy these conditions, so the same threshold applies to estimated whitening in that setting. For the shifted-lognormal law, α c W \alpha_{c}^{\rm W} is the ideal-whitening reference; their bounded-spectrum assumptions do not directly cover the estimated-whitening algorithm, whose performance is shown empirically.

sections.heading: Relation to the masking and Bayes thresholds.
sections.text: Our replica analysis connects this established whitening threshold to dynamic masking. Combining the Bayes expression ( F.67 ) with the lower bound in ( D.48 ), specialized to dynamic linear masking in ( D.133 ), gives α c BO = 1 β 2 ​ 𝔼 γ ​ [ γ − 2 ] ≤ α c W = 1 β 2 ​ 𝔼 γ ​ [ γ − 1 ] 2 ≤ α c , RS dyn . \alpha_{c}^{\rm BO}=\frac{1}{\beta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}[\gamma^{-2}]}\leq\alpha_{c}^{\rm W}=\frac{1}{\beta^{2}\mathbb{E}_{\gamma}[\gamma^{-1}]^{2}}\leq\alpha_{c,\mathrm{RS}}^{\rm dyn}. (H.1) The inverse moments are finite for both displayed laws. The first inequality is strict for a nonconstant variance law by Cauchy–Schwarz. It orders the recovery onsets; the relative alignments above threshold are assessed by the simulations. Thus masking can outperform diagonal correction while remaining less effective than whitening at the onset of recovery.

sections.heading: H.5 Dynamic masking and nonlinear autoencoders
sections.text: Figure 9: Masking improves recovery across activation functions. Cosine similarity for (a) dynamic masking and (b) no masking in the same setting as Fig. 3 . Colored curves are replica predictions, colored markers in both panels are ERM simulations at finite d = 2000 d=2000 , averaged across 30 30 seeds ± 1 \pm 1 SD. In both panels, the green curve shows the Bayes-optimal prediction and green diamonds show AMP results ( Secs. F.5 and H.14 ). Fig. 9 compares dynamic masking with the no-masking reconstruction, Eq. 5 , for linear, ReLU, ELU, and tanh activations. We use the same setting as Fig. 3 . Across the four activations, dynamic masking develops substantially higher alignment, whereas full reconstruction retains low mean alignment throughout the displayed range. Thus, changing the activation of the unmasked autoencoder does not help to recover the spike. On the other hand, for dynamic masking, linear, ELU, and tanh dynamic curves are close, while ReLU requires larger sample complexity to attain comparable alignment.

sections.text: Fig. 11 varies the number of independently labeled examples used to fit the frozen scalar logistic probe. We reuse the linear dynamic-masking replica solution from Fig. 3 , with bounded noise, β = 1 \beta=1 , ρ = 0.75 \rho=0.75 , and λ R = 10 − 4 \lambda_{R}=10^{-4} , and evaluate ( G.15 ) for n ds ∈ [ 1,128 ] n_{\rm ds}\in[1,128] . sections.heading: H.8 Early-stopping without masking
sections.text: Figs. 12 and 13 evaluate frozen linear probes at intermediate unmasked-pretraining checkpoints for the architectures and datasets of Fig. 1 . In both architectures, training and validation reconstruction MSE continue to improve after downstream accuracy has peaked. The deterioration in the representation is therefore not accompanied by a rise in held-out reconstruction error. Figure 12: Better reconstruction need not improve CNN representations. sections.heading: H.9 Mask renewal and image augmentation in CNNs
sections.text: Fig. 14 complements Fig. 5 using the CNN autoencoder on CIFAR-10 from Fig. 1 (b). We compare static and dynamic masking with and without stochastic cropping and flipping, averaging over five seeds. Within each seed, the four conditions share the data split and initial autoencoder weights. The architecture, optimizer settings, validation-based checkpoint selection and stopping rule, and frozen linear-probing protocol follow Sec. H.1 . Figure 14: Mask renewal and image augmentation in CNNs. Frozen linear-probe test top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10 versus masking ratio ρ \rho . Blue/yellow indicate dynamic / static masking; circles/crosses denote pretraining without/with stochastic cropping and flipping. Each marker reports the mean over five seeds, with data splits and autoencoder initializations shared across conditions within each seed. Linear probes use no image augmentation. Cropping and flipping substantially improve static masking across the sweep, bringing its mean accuracy close to dynamic masking at lower masking ratios. At larger masking ratios, dynamic masking retains an advantage even with augmentation. The CNN comparison therefore supports the same interpretation as the ViT experiment: geometric transformations can partly compensate for mask reuse by changing the content to be predicted. The remaining gap shows that the extent of this compensation depends on the masking ratio and experimental setting.

sections.heading: H.10 CNN training budgets and validation selection
sections.text: We examine the CNN mask-diversity comparison of Fig. 4 (b) at ρ = 0.625 \rho=0.625 , with K ∈ { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , 16 , 32 } K\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} and dynamic masking. Both experiments use the CIFAR-10 architecture, AdamW settings, and the frozen linear-probing protocol of Sec. H.1 , without cropping or flipping. Each condition has five seeds (different pretraining/validation splits). Encoders are selected by validation reconstruction MSE followed by downstream accuracy measured on a separate test set. Fig. 15 shows the original training and validation trajectories with the plateau learning-rate (LR) scheduler. Finite-mask runs continue reducing training error after validation error levels off or rises ( overfitting ), motivating validation-based checkpoint selection. Since the original scheduler operates in epochs whose update counts depend on K K , we also test whether the results persist under a common schedule measured in optimizer updates. To assess the role of the scheduler, we repeat the experiments with the same data splits, random seeds, and initial weights, using a fixed learning rate (LR) of 10 − 3 10^{-3} and a longer training number of optimizer updates ( Fig. 16 ). All conditions now use 2,500 2{,}500 updates between validation evaluations, a stopping patience of 125,000 125{,}000 updates without improvement, and a total maximum of 1,150,000 1{,}150{,}000 updates. Fig. 17 (a) compares validation-selected (early-stopped checkpoints) encoders under the two protocols. Their mean test accuracies remain close across masking conditions, and the downstream improvement with mask diversity persists under the fixed-learning-rate control. The extended runs also exhibit a reconstruction-generalization gap. This changes the checkpoint used for downstream evaluation, not the training or stopping procedure. Thus, the downstream mask-diversity trend persists both when selecting the encoder by validation reconstruction MSE and when selecting its checkpoint at a common training step. sections.heading: H.11 Numerical assessment of finite-mask threshold ratios
sections.text: How well does the weak-signal mask-reuse law describe recovery at finite signal strength? Fig. 18 compares it with thresholds computed from the full linear equations at zero ridge. We solve the uninformative closures in ( D.12 )–( D.16 ) and locate the gain crossing in ( D.23 ); Sec. H.12 gives the numerical procedure.

sections.heading: Variance laws and normalization.
sections.text: The two rows of Fig. 18 use homogeneous noise, γ = 1 \gamma=1 , and the bounded law γ = 1 + c ⁡ ( 9 4 ​ B − 3 4 ) , B ∼ Beta ⁡ ( 1 , 2 ) , c ≃ 0.5743390142 . \gamma=1+c\left(\frac{9}{4}B-\frac{3}{4}\right),\qquad B\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,2),\qquad c\simeq 0.5743390142. sections.heading: H.13 Mask diversity in BERT
sections.text: We compare one fixed mask per sequence ( K = 1 K=1 ), a fixed collection of ten masks ( K = 10 K=10 ), and dynamic mask resampling in a BERT-Medium pretraining pilot. Each condition uses three pretraining seeds and two fine-tuning seeds per pretraining seed and task. The corpus, architecture, and pretraining budget are shared across masking conditions.

sections.heading: Implementation and data.
sections.text: We train a BERT-style masked language model [ 23 ] using our adaptation of DinkyTrain 5 5 5 https://github.com/princeton-nlp/DinkyTrain . [ 54 ] , built on fairseq [ 45 ] and its RoBERTa implementation [ 38 ] . DinkyTrain’s efficient pretraining recipe builds on Izsak et al. [30] . The pre-LayerNorm encoder has eight layers, hidden dimension 512 512 , feed-forward dimension 2048 2048 , eight attention heads, and approximately 51.5 51.5 million pretraining parameters. We use the repository’s preprocessed Wikipedia–BookCorpus data [ 62 ] , with GPT-2 byte-pair encoding and a 50,265 50{,}265 -token model vocabulary. The pilot uses one fixed shard, retaining 3,756,032 3{,}756{,}032 contiguous sequences of length 128 128 . Token blocks are constructed before mask views are assigned; the underlying text remains fixed across presentations.

sections.heading: Masking protocol.
sections.text: We select 15 % 15\% of token positions for prediction. Every selected token is replaced by [MASK] ; neither random-token substitution nor unchanged selected tokens are used. For finite K K , the corruption depends on the mask seed, sequence identifier, and view identifier, and is fixed across presentations. Dynamic masking draws a fresh corruption at each presentation. Each sequence is presented 109 109 times in every condition: the single K = 1 K=1 mask is reused throughout, the ten K = 10 K=10 masks are reused approximately eleven times each, and dynamic masking draws 109 109 masks. Pretraining seeds are 0 , 1 , 2 0,1,2 , with the training and mask seed both set to the same value. Seeds control initialization, data order, dropout, and mask draws. Held-out validation uses 1,941 1{,}941 sequences.

sections.heading: Pretraining budget and optimization.
sections.text: Each run completes 99,953 99{,}953 optimizer updates with an effective batch size of 4,096 4{,}096 . Adam uses a peak learning rate of 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} , 1,999 1{,}999 warmup updates followed by cosine decay, coefficients ( 0.9 , 0.98 ) (0.9,0.98) , ϵ = 10 − 6 \epsilon=10^{-6} , weight decay 0.01 0.01 , and no gradient clipping. sections.heading: Downstream optimization.
sections.text: We fine-tune the full model on eight GLUE tasks [ 53 ] for ten epochs and evaluate after the last epoch on the development split. The maximum input length is 512 512 tokens. Learning rate and batch size are 10 − 5 10^{-5} and 32 32 for MNLI, QNLI, QQP, and SST-2; 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} and 16 16 for STS-B; and 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} and 16 16 for MRPC, CoLA, and RTE. For MRPC, CoLA, and RTE, a preliminary learning-rate sweep resolved the majority-class predictions observed with the initial fine-tuning settings. We selected 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} using the K = 10 K=10 model with pretraining seed 0 from { 5 × 10 − 5 , 10 − 4 , 2 × 10 − 4 , 4 × 10 − 4 } \{5\times 10^{-5},10^{-4},2\times 10^{-4},4\times 10^{-4}\} and applied it across all masking conditions and seeds. This value is included in the released fine-tuning grid accompanying the compact BERT models of Turc et al. [51] . 6 6 6 https://github.com/google-research/bert . Adam uses coefficients ( 0.9 , 0.98 ) (0.9,0.98) , ϵ = 10 − 6 \epsilon=10^{-6} , weight decay 0.1 0.1 , and no gradient clipping. The learning rate warms up for 6 % 6\% of the update budget and then decays linearly. Dropout and attention dropout are both 0.1 0.1 . Classification tasks use cross-entropy; STS-B uses mean-squared-error regression.

sections.heading: Downstream performance.
sections.text: In Table 5 , K = 10 K=10 improves the mean score over K = 1 K=1 on all eight tasks. Dynamic masking has the highest mean on seven of eight tasks, including both MNLI splits. The additional gain over K = 10 K=10 depends on the task: the MRPC means are nearly equal, while RTE remains weak and variable. The results support a benefit of mask diversity across independent pretraining runs.
